64 Chapter 5. Conclusions Smoke points of microgravity and normal gravity gas-jet diffusion flames were observed. Microgravity conditions emphasized small burners and effects of coflow velocity. These flames allow extensive control of residence time, which may be important in smoke point phenomena. An increase in coflow velocity increases the smoke point length. A decrease in burner diameter increases the smoke point length. These two effects can be explained qualitatively by considering residence times; increased fuel and/or coflow velocities yield increased smoke point lengths. The effect of coflow velocity could also be explained by increased O2 transport if soot oxidation downstream of the flame sheet is transport limited. The fuel sooting propensities in these flames are as follows: propane < ethylene < 50% propylene < 75% propylene < propylene, however ethylene is less sooty than propane for the 0.76 mm burner. To the first order, luminous length at the smoke point is proportional to fuel mass flow rate, consistent with past theory and experiments. A second-order effect is that this length increases for low ua,o / uf,o velocity ratios. Flames of this nature approximate the behavior of a jet flame in still air. Smoke points of normal gravity gas-jet diffusion flames were also observed. For the smaller burner tests in a confined coflow environment, smoke point length increased with an increase in coflow velocity or a decrease in nozzle diameter. For a very large burner in an unconfined coflow, the smoke point length decreased with increasing

65 coflow velocity for propylene and ethylene, but increased for propane. This, and results of a previous study showing domains where the smoke point is invariant to changes in coflow velocity, indicate that the relationship of smoke point to coflow velocity and nozzle diameter is more complicated than initially expected. It has been hypothesized that the different responses may be due to different soot oxidation regimes, transport-limited, kinetics-limited, and residence-time-limited. Simplified analysis of the residence time and soot formation time to soot oxidation time ratio of the SPICE microgravity flames failed to yield substantial collapse of the smoke point data or a residence time related criticality. This may be due to the simplified nature of the analysis, such as neglecting combustion related volumetric expansion. COMSOL® simulations have shown that the simplified Schlichting-based analysis does not adequately predict the centerline velocity decay of air jets with initial air to fuel velocity ratios larger than around 0.2 – 0.5. However there is evidence that the analysis would more adequately predict the centerline velocity decay of jets with an initial uniform flow. This current study has not proven a particular smoke point mechanism. It has shown that the smoke point depends on choice of coflow velocity and burner diameter; these factors cannot be assumed away as negligible. The coflow jet flame geometry is perhaps not tractable enough to lend itself to fundamental analysis of sooting phenomena. Given that a smoke point depends on a large number of inputs, more rigorous controls would be necessary to isolate particular factors. It is hoped;

66 however, given the results shown and the hypotheses presented, a more defined experimental procedure could be developed to directly influence and measure residence times, formation rates, and oxidation rates as they relate to the smoke point and sooting phenomena.

Maryland Project Scientist: Zengguang Yuan, National Center for Space Exploration Research Project Manager: Robert Hawersaat NASA GRC I. Introduction A. Hypothesis The hypothesis of the SPICE investigation is that smoke point behavior will be observed for co-flowing flames and that it will show dependence on nozzle diameter and coflow velocity. B. Objectives of Investigation The objective of the SPICE experiment is to find the laminar smoke-point properties of nonbuoyant jet diffusion flames (i.e., the properties of the largest laminar jet diffusion flames that do not emit soot) for several fuels under different nozzle diameter/ co-flow velocity configurations. Luminous flame shape measurements would also be made to verify models of the flame shapes under co-flow conditions. C. Previous Mission Experience N/A D. Background/History of Project (Optional) The SPICE experiment was an outgrowth of the Laminar Soot Processes Experiment (LSP) which flew on STS 83, 94, and 107. SPICE utilized the design heritage and modified the hardware from the Enclosed Laminar Flames Experiment (ELF) which flew in the Middeck Glovebox on STS 87. II. Methods/Research Operations A. Discussion of Method/Protocol Most tests were conducted by setting the coflow velocity, igniting the flame, and adjusting the fuel flow rate. Approximate smoke points were identified in the video by the flight crew and simultaneously by the ground support crew in Cleveland. Typical burn times were 60 s, and after each two such burns the MSG contents were flushed with ISS cabin air. After the tests the video record was analyzed to

List of Preflight, In-flight, Postflight Anomalies SPICE operated very successfully with the only significant anomaly being the accumulation of soot in the outlet screen which changed the flow behavior in the duct. Urbanc aDepartment of Fire Protection Engineering, University of Maryland, College Park, MD, USA bNational Center for Space Exploration Research, Cleveland, OH, USA cNASA Glenn Research Center, Cleveland, OH, USA Laminar smoke points were measured in nonbuoyant laminar jet diffusion flames in air coflow aboard the International Space Station as part of the Smoke Points in Coflow Experiment (SPICE). Smoke points were found for ethylene, propane, propylene, and mixtures of 50 and 75% propylene by volume in nitrogen. Burner diameters were 0.41, 0.76 and 1.6 mm and coflow velocities varied from 5.4 – 65 cm/s. These flames afford good control over residence time via variations in dilution, burner diameter, and coflow velocity. Increasing coflow velocity decreases luminous flame lengths, but moves smoke points to higher fuel flow rates and longer luminous flame lengths. Smaller burners have longer smoke points for coflowing flames. These trends can be explained qualitatively by considering total residence time effects. The luminous flame lengths generally correlate with fuel mass flow rate divided by stoichiometric mixture fraction, although they increase slightly as air velocity decreases. 1. Introduction Soot formation is an important unresolved problem in combustion science. Soot is estimated to be responsible for up to 50,000 premature deaths in the U.S. [1] and is believed to contribute to climate change and glacial melting [2]. Radiation from soot in flames allows reading by candlelight but

is an important unresolved problem in combustion science. Soot is estimated to be responsible for up to 50,000 premature deaths in the U.S. [1] and is believed to contribute to climate change and glacial melting [2]. Radiation from soot in flames allows reading by candlelight but also contributes to heat loads in engines and the spread of unwanted fires. Smoking flames emit carbon monoxide, which is the major cause of death in fires [3]. The smoke point is the condition (or length) where a flame begins to emit soot. Smoke points indicate the sooting propensity of a fuel in diffusion flames. In normal gravity, laminar smoke points have been measured for many gaseous and condensed fuels [4–9]. Laminar smoke points have been found to correlate with soot volume fractions [10] and radiative loss factions [11] of turbulent diffusion flames. Yang et al. [12] found that gas turbine soot emissions correlate very well with a threshold sooting index (TSI) based on fuel molecular weight divided by the laminar smoke point. Smoke points have been shown to correlate with the smoke release from turbulent buoyant flames [13] and have been applied to developing general soot models for computational combustion simulations [14] and heat release measurements [15]. In a 1988 paper [16], Glassman predicted that smoke points would not occur in nonbuoyant gasjet flames. He based this on the assumption that residence time scales with the square root of fuel flow rate in normal gravity but is independent of flow rate in microgravity flames. Subsequent work [17] observed smoke points of nonbuoyant flames aboard a parabolic aircraft and used numerical predictions to

this on the assumption that residence time scales with the square root of fuel flow rate in normal gravity but is independent of flow rate in microgravity flames. Subsequent work [17] observed smoke points of nonbuoyant flames aboard a parabolic aircraft and used numerical predictions to show that residence time increases with flame length for nonbuoyant flames without co-flow. Urban et al. [18] reported smoke points of microgravity flames observed on a space shuttle. Microgravity smoke point measurements are difficult in parabolic aircraft

2 owing to g-jitter and in drop facilities owing to limited test times. Attributing smoke point behavior to total residence time helps with qualitative explanations of smoke point behavior but to date has not yielded successful quantitative correlations [8]. This may be because smoke points arise from a competition between the times available for soot formation and soot oxidation. Delichatsios and co-workers suggested that smoke point length is proportional to soot formation time [19–20]. Quantitative correlations may also be possible from an examination of radiative losses, which have been observed to be 20 – 30% for normal-gravity smoke point flames and to increase with adiabatic flame temperature [5]. Soot is transported in flames by convection and thermophoresis. By varying the burner diameter, coflow velocity, and fuel dilution, flame shape and residence times in the soot formation and soot oxidation regions can be changed. A decrease in coflow velocity will generally increase entrainment of flow towards the flame axis. Kent and Wagner [21] found that smoke burn out in the oxidative region of the flame ceases when the tip of a buoyant diffusion flame cools to approximately 1300 K. Urban et al. [22] found that the tip of a nonbuoyant (microgravity) flame reaches 1000 K at its smoke point. In buoyant flames this decrease in temperature is attributed primarily to heat conduction, while in nonbuoyant flames it is attributed largely to radiative quenching [23]. The radiative quenching effect causes a visible tip opening in nonbuoyant smoke points of flames of relatively long residence time [22]. A recent 2.5 s drop tower study by Jeon et al. [24] found that for

nonbuoyant flames it is attributed largely to radiative quenching [23]. The radiative quenching effect causes a visible tip opening in nonbuoyant smoke points of flames of relatively long residence time [22]. A recent 2.5 s drop tower study by Jeon et al. [24] found that for small coflow velocities the soot volume fraction increases with coflow velocity. This was attributed to an increase in temperature. Lin and Faeth [7,25] studied the effects of coflow velocity on weakly-buoyant flames near the smoke point. They observed flames in normal gravity, but at low pressures to reduce the effects of gravity. They found that increasing the coflow velocity reduced soot volume fractions and increased the smoke point length. This was attributed to decreased flame residence time and modified soot pathlines. Refs. [7 and 24] both showed that luminous flame lengths decrease with increasing coflow velocity. Their burner diameters, 7 and 10 mm, respectively, were much larger than those considered here. Thus motivated, the objectives of this study are: 1. to measure nonbuoyant smoke points of propane, ethylene, propylene, and propylene/nitrogen mixtures, 2. to identify the effects of coflow velocity and burner diameter on the smoke points, and 3. to correlate the luminous flame lengths. 2. Experimental The Smoke Points in Coflow Experiment (SPICE) module was brought to the International Space Station (ISS) in 2008. It was operated in the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) by various crew members in 2009. Smoke points were attempted for all fuels for fuel jet diameters of 0.41, 0.76, and 1.6 mm. The conditions for which smoke points were found are summarized in Table 1. In some cases (e.g., tests involving ethylene) the fuel supply was depleted before desired smoke points could be found, as the supply was limited to two 75 cc bottles of each fuel at gage pressures of 760 – 1440 kPa, depending on the fuel. The SPICE module contains a rectangular duct that has an approximately 76 mm square cross section with rounded corners. A DC fan supplies coflowing air from the glovebox contents. The air passes through a honeycomb and screen to reduce swirl and then enters the duct. The air and combustion products leave the duct through a perforated copper plate followed by a copper screen. The screen is 50 mm upstream of the burner discharge and the plate is 120 mm downstream. Fan voltage is varied to control the coflow velocity, which is measured

Fan voltage is varied to control the coflow velocity, which is measured with a hotwire anemometer between the inlet honeycomb and screen. This anemometer was calibrated in normal gravity using a hot-wire anemometer 36 mm downstream of the duct entrance. Fuel flow rate was adjusted manually and controlled with a mass flow meter. The flames were ignited with a hot-wire ignitor. Video was recorded with an analog color video camera and downlinked in real time. Still images were recorded with a 12 bit Nikon™ D100 single-lens reflex color digital still camera (with 3008 × 2000 pixels) with a 60 mm lens. Results and Discussion Some smoke points, propane and ethylene in particular, were identified by the onset of gradual (rather than sharp) dimming and reddening of the luminous flame tip in the downstream direction. Rounding of the tip also was associated with the smoke point. For conditions sufficiently above the smoke point, quenched soot could be seen leaving the flame. The brightest flames did not always display significant reddening or darkening near their tips, except well above the smoke point. This occurred for the pure propylene and propylene mixtures, and the smoke point was identified by the rapid transition to an open-tipped, soot emitting flame. The flames generally reached steady conditions within 5 s of ignition or a change in flow rate of fuel or air. Flames of propylene and propylene mixtures were generally more luminous than those of methane, ethylene, and propane, attributed to their higher propensity to form soot. The smoke point transition was more abrupt in the propylene-based fuels than for propane or ethylene. Periodic flame motion was observed in some flames, especially those with high coflow, long length, and low fuel velocity, and is attributed to non-uniform coflow. This effect was small and did not prevent clear measurement of flame length. Figure 1 shows images for representative flames near their smoke points. For a given choice of fuel and burner diameter, an increase in coflow velocity generally increases the smoke point length. This behavior is attributed to decreased residence times in the soot formation region when coflow velocity is increased. The variation of smoke point with coflow velocity is greater for longer flames. Figure 2 reveals that smoke points of coflowing nonbuoyant flames increase with decreasing burner diameter. Conclusions Smoke points of microgravity gas-jet diffusion flames were observed. Conditions emphasized small burners and effects of coflow velocity. These flames allow extensive control of residence time, which is important in smoke point phenomena. The major conclusions are as follows. 1. An increase in coflow velocity increases the smoke point length. 2. A decrease in burner diameter increases the smoke point length. 3. These two effects can be explained qualitatively by considering residence times; increased fuel and/or coflow velocities yield increased smoke point lengths. Figure 2. ii Smoke Point in Co-flow Experiment (SPICE) Abstract The laminar smoke point is the condition (and the luminous flame length) where a flame begins to emit soot. Smoke points indicate the sooting propensity of a fuel in diffusion flames. In normal gravity, laminar smoke points have been measured for many gaseous and condensed fuels. Laminar smoke points have been found to correlate with soot volume fractions and radiative loss fractions of turbulent diffusion flames. SPICE project measured laminar smoke points in nonbuoyant laminar jet diffusion flames in co-flowing air aboard the International Space Station. Fifty-two smoke points were found for ethylene, propane, propylene, and propylene/nitrogen mixtures. Burner diameters were 0.41, 0.76, and 1.6 mm and co-flow velocities varied from 5.4 – 65 cm/s. These flames afford extensive control over residence time via variations in dilution, burner diameter, and co-flow velocity. Increasing co-flow velocity decreases luminous flame lengths, but moves smoke points to higher fuel flow rates and longer luminous flame lengths. Smaller burners have longer smoke points for co-flowing flames. These trends can be explained qualitatively by considering total residence time effects. The luminous flame lengths generally correlate with fuel mass flow rate divided by stoichiometric mixture fraction, although they increase slightly as air velocity decreases. The measured smoke point lengths were found to correlate with burner diameter to the –0.91 power times coflow velocity to the 0.41 power. The measurements allow estimates of pseudo threshold soot indices (TSI) for microgravity diffusion flames, indicating an unusually high sooting propensity for propane in microgravity. A model of residence times in coflowing flames is developed, and although residence time helps explain

coflow velocity to the 0.41 power. The measurements allow estimates of pseudo threshold soot indices (TSI) for microgravity diffusion flames, indicating an unusually high sooting propensity for propane in microgravity. A model of residence times in coflowing flames is developed, and although residence time helps explain many of the observations, it does not correlate the measured smoke points. The measurements yielded estimates of sooting propensities of the present fuels in microgravity diffusion flames. Acknowledgments The authors acknowledge G.M. 1 INTRODUCTION SPICE project, from it was rewarded in 1997 to it was conducted onboard ISS in 2009, covered more than a decade time span. Faeth of the University of Michigan for his proposal titled as Laminar Smoke Point Properties of Nonbuoyant Round-Jet Diffusion Flames in response to NASA’s 1996 Solicitation for Glovebox Investigations issued in late 1996. Various project reviews necessary for the flight project, were completed. What Follows is the science significance and justification of the SPICE project. Soot formation in hydrocarbon-fueled flames is an important unresolved problem in combustion science. Soot is estimated to be responsible for up to 52,000 premature deaths annually in the U.S.1 and is believed to contribute to climate change and glacial melting.2 Radiation from soot in flames is beneficial in many applications but also contributes to unwanted heat loads in engines and the spread of fires. Carbon monoxide emitted by smoking flames is the major cause of death in fires.3 Knowledge of Soot formation is needed for developing computational combustion.

2 The differences between soot processes in buoyant and nonbuoyant laminar jet diffusion flames can be seen by comparing their soot production regions as plotted in Fig. 1. Soot formation in diffusion flames generally is limited to fuel-equivalence ratios, φ, in the range 1-2, which are marked on the plots. Unlike gases, which both convect and diffuse, soot mainly convects with the flow velocity so that it moves along the streamline. For buoyant flames, the dividing streamline generally is inside the soot formation region so that most of the soot initially forms near the flame sheet, where φ, =1, and then moves radially inward toward cooler regions having higher fuel concentrations. The soot formation process for nonbuoyant flames is completely different: most of the soot initially forms near the cool core of the flame, where φ is close to 2, and is drawn directly toward the flame sheet. Results from an MSL-1 combustion project, the Laminar Soot Processes (LSP), revealed that the smoke height phenomenon in microgravity can be substantially different form that seen in normal gravity. The removal of buoyancy induced acceleration can cause the smoke point phenomenon to be dominated by radiative heat losses for conditions of low overall flame velocity. Under these conditions the flame extinguishes at the flame tip allowing soot to be emitted. In spite of this effect, it is still possible to have flames that either emit soot along all stream lines or do not emit soot anywhere, for conditions where radiation losses do not dominate. Soot path lines through buoyant and non-buoyant flames The information of smoke-point properties and flame shapes is needed to improve our understanding of heat and mass transfer mechanisms for different flame conditions. Unfortunately, while the laminar smoke-point properties of buoyant jet diffusion flames at normal gravity are well known, corresponding information for nonbuoyant flames is limited and questionable. Thus the insights of soot generation and oxidation processes under microgravity conditions are critical to devise better fire safety strategy in spacecraft needed for long term space travels and other space exploration activities. In addition, the improved understanding of soot processes in laminar flames will help us, by analogy, to gain better understanding of soot processes in practical turbulent flames. The objectives of the SPICE experiments is to find the laminar smoke-point properties of nonbuoyant jet diffusion flames for several fuels under different nozzle diameter/co-flow velocity configurations. Luminous flame shape measurements would also be made to verify models of the

3 flame shapes under co-flow conditions. In particular, the experiments are planned to be conducted under the following conditions: six types of fuels: methane, ethylene, propane, propylene, 75% propylene mixed with 25% nitrogen in moles, and 50% propylene mixed with 50% nitrogen in moles; three nozzles: 0.4, 0.8 and 1.6 mm ID and two air velocities: 100% and 50% of the maximum air flow velocity (near 50cm/s). The operation procedures are as such that the air velocity is set first, then start the fuel flow and ignite the flame. Fuel flow rate is adjusted until the smoke point is reached. Thus, for each combination of a fuel and a nozzle size, two smoke point fuel flow rates are obtained. One is under 100% air velocity and the other is under 50% air velocity. Then in the case of 50% air velocity, the fuel flow rate is reduced to 50% of the smoke point fuel flow rate to get a flame length with that fuel flow rate. SPICE EXPERIMENT SETUP A. The module is also equipped with data logger and PCMCIA storage. B. Air velocity distribution in the flow duct An important feature of SPICE is that it has air co-flow surrounding the flames. SPICE is the first experiment that studies soot processes of laminar jet diffusion flame under long term microgravity condition with air coflow. Because the velocity distribution in or near the flame is complicated by the varying gas property and thermal expansion, the coflow air velocity can only be specified in far field and the inlet of the flow duct as boundary conditions of the flame under investigation. For this reason, the information of air velocity distribution before igniting of the flame is needed. The air velocity was measured with an anemometer at different locations in the flow duct at different fan speed. SPICE FLIGHT TESTS The actual SPICE tests were conducted in SMG in twelve sessions from February 14, 2009 to June 23, 2009. In each session, the SPICE science team and engineering team were in the TeleScience Center (TSC) in GRC to support the tests conducted on MSG. 17 DISCUSSION Although it is convenient to classified all flames, laminar vs. turbulent and diffusion vs. premixed, into two categories based on their soot emission conditions, i.e., soot emitting flames and non-soot emitting flames, the conditions delineating the two or the conditions of onset of soot emission are difficult to define. Up to date, these conditions have been documented solely based on experimental observations. Many efforts have been made to develop a universal method of defining the onset of soot emission, i.e., smoke point, conditions, in terms of primary parameters of the flame. But none of these efforts has been quite successful yet. The primary parameters of the flame mentioned here refer to parameters used to set the flame, not those generated by the flame. The primary parameters of jet diffusion flames include fuel type, fuel and oxidizer supply rates, ambient temperature and pressure, and configuration of the device where the flame takes place, such as nozzle diameter and dimensions of the combustion chamber. The flame temperature, gas velocity and species distributions as well as flame shapes and derived parameters such as heat generation and heat loss, are the parameters generated by the flame which is not considered as primary parameters. If a method that relates smoke point to those primary parameters were found, we would be able to predict whether a flame emits soot or not based on the planned flame conditions. In the course of pursuing such a universal method, a number of surmises of the mechanism of soot emission have been proposed to associate smoke point with certain flame generated parameters. Those surmises served as a

In the course of pursuing such a universal method, a number of surmises of the mechanism of soot emission have been proposed to associate smoke point with certain flame generated parameters. Those surmises served as a middle step in hoping to help further development of the aforementioned method. The first surmise, and least controversial, is that smoke points occur when soot temperature drops below a critical temperature prior to soot burnout. This temperature is about 1300 K in normal gravity8,9 and 1000 K in microgravity.10,11 The second is that smoke point occurs when radiative loss fraction reaches 0.2 – 0.4 for normal-gravity flames12-16 or 0.4 – 0.6 for microgravity flames.17 Since the radiative fraction of heat loss increases with fuel flow rate, smoke point will occur as the fuel flow rate is higher than Figure 19. 18 certain value. This is consistent with experimental observations. The third surmise is that the smoke point correlates to the ratio of luminous length divided by stoichiometric length. This ratio increases with flow rate. Once it reaches about 2, smoke point occurs.15,18,19 The last surmise suggests that smoke point correlates with the centerline flame residence time. This is the most complex8-11,17,18,2024 surmise because flame residence time affects the soot processes in twofold. An increase in residence time can lead to soot emissions by increasing the time available for soot formation. Because this generally also increases the time available for soot oxidation, it has been proposed that smoke points are associated with conditions where the time available for soot formation exceeds that for soot oxidation to certain extent.21 This is difficult to prove because to evaluate the flame residence time requires the velocity distribution alone the centerline and the flame length, both of which are resulted flame parameters, not readily available from primary parameters of the experiment. In addition, the soot formation time and oxidation time are conceptually defined. Practically, these times are not measurable and they might be overlapped, i.e., for the same soot aggregate, adding and oxidizing carbon particles may happen simultaneously. Because of these difficulties and ambiguities, the fame residence time theory cannot be proved or disproved rigorously. However, these obstacles do not prevent us from checking the residence time theory against the observed smoke point data with the help of some approximated velocity distribution and flame length information. CLOSING REMARKS Smoke points of 55 microgravity gas-jet diffusion flames in coflowing air were measured in earth orbit. The conditions emphasized small burners and the effects of coflow velocity. These flames allow extensive control over residence time, which is important in smoke point phenomena. The major conclusions are as follows: 1. An increase in coflow velocity increases the smoke point length. 2. A decrease in burner diameter increases the smoke point length. 3. These two effects can be explained qualitatively by considering residence times; increased fuel and/or coflow velocities yield increased smoke point lengths. 4. The sooting propensities of the present fuel mixtures in microgravity increase according to ethylene < propane < 50% propylene < 75% propylene < propylene. This is the same as in normal gravity except for the exchanged positions of ethylene and propane. 5. Consistent with past theory and experiments, luminous length at the smoke point is proportional to fuel mass flow rate. However there is a slight increase in luminous length as ua / uf decreases. 6. Although residence time is helpful in understanding the present smoke points, it does not yield quantitative correlations of smoke points. 7. The present smoke point lengths

Overview The Cool Flames Investigation with Gases (CFI-G) experiment is one of six independent experiments that make up the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project for which the tests were conducted within the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station (ISS). The experiment’s Principal Investigator (PI) is Prof. Peter B. Sunderland of the Department of Fire Protection Engineering at the University of Maryland. The two Co-Investigators (Co-Is) are Profs. Richard L. Axelbaum and Forman A. Williams who are respectively from the Washington University of St. Louis and the University of California, San Diego (UCSD). Meanwhile, Dennis P. Stocker of the NASA Glenn Research Center is the Project Scientist (PS) for ACME including CFI-G and the rest of the ACME investigations. In ACME’s preparatory drop testing, etc., Dr. Fumiaki Takahashi of the Case Western Reserve University (CWRU) served as the Deputy Project Scientist. For ACME’s spaceflight operations, the NASA science team included Drs. Uday G. Hegde and Vedha Nayagam who are also with CWRU. The ISS operations for CFI-G were conducted from March to Oct. 2021 in two sequential rounds of testing. The two rounds occurred during Increments 64-65 and 65-66 and respectively featured normal and inverse flames. The inverse flame tests were conducted with the chamber filled with a mixture of nitrogen and gaseous fuel while an oxygen/nitrogen mixture flowed from the burner. As a result, the inverse flames were effectively inside out, e.g., where the soot formed outside rather than inside of the flames. Although it was in the second round, the final day of CFI-G

nitrogen and gaseous fuel while an oxygen/nitrogen mixture flowed from the burner. As a result, the inverse flames were effectively inside out, e.g., where the soot formed outside rather than inside of the flames. Although it was in the second round, the final day of CFI-G testing was carried out in the normal flame configuration, with gaseous fuel (with or without nitrogen) flowing into an oxygen/nitrogen atmosphere. This was an added test day carried out under conditions in which low-temperature combustion occurred during the first round of testing. CFI-G was a late addition to ACME, where the experiment was jointly selected for spaceflight by the National Science Foundation (NSF) and the Center for the Advancement of Science in Space (CASIS) rather than NASA. The selection was notably announced after the core ACME hardware had launched to the ISS and just weeks before ACME’s on-orbit operations began. It is effectively an extension of ACME’s Flame Design experiment for which the PI and Co-I are respectively Axelbaum and Sunderland. And it is likewise a follow-on to the Cool Flames Investigation (CFI), led by Williams, in which liquid droplets were burned rather than gaseous fuel. Although CFI-G wasn’t selected for spaceflight by NASA, its ISS operations and the development of its unique hardware, software, and procedure were carried out by the same teams of personnel as the other ACME experiments, primarily from ZIN Technologies, Inc.

Background This background is the Project Summary from the experiment’s 2017 proposal in response to a solicitation from the NSF/CASIS Collaboration on Combustion and Thermal Transport Processes Research on the International Space Station to Benefit Life on Earth. Overview: Cool diffusion flames were discovered in 2012 aboard the ISS. This spawned a rapidly growing research field, but only a small number of measurements at limited conditions are available. Consequently, cool flame kinetics mechanisms cannot be adequately tested or advanced. This could be impeding the development of cleaner and more efficient internal combustion engines. It is proposed here to observe cool diffusion flames supported by porous spherical burners fed with propane, n-butane, and n-pentane. Normal and inverse flames will be considered for a broad range of dilution conditions and pressures. The ISS is the ideal platform for observing cool diffusion flames because they typically require 20 s to establish and they could burn indefinitely. Tests will be performed using the ACME insert in the CIR. Minimal hardware development will be required because the spherical porous burners and gas delivery system will be those used by the Flame Design flight experiment, while the diagnostics will be those used by the CFI flight experiment. The objectives are to observe diverse cool diffusion flames aboard the ISS, to simulate the tests with an advanced CFD model, and to identify or develop a chemical kinetics mechanism that accurately models these conditions. Intellectual Merit: Most internal combustion engines are designed using computer models that neglect cool flame chemistry, but ignition and flame propagation

the ISS, to simulate the tests with an advanced CFD model, and to identify or develop a chemical kinetics mechanism that accurately models these conditions. Intellectual Merit: Most internal combustion engines are designed using computer models that neglect cool flame chemistry, but ignition and flame propagation in engines depend on cool flame chemistry. Cool flame chemistry also has a significant impact on fuel octane and cetane numbers, whose understanding has large economic consequences. The proposed experiments will take advantage of many state-of-the-art diagnostics that are already available on the ISS. The flame system to be studied will allow steady spherical cool diffusion flames to be observed for the first time. An advanced CFD model will simulate the flames and will aid the testing and development of cool flame kinetics models. Observing cool flames burning as steady spherical diffusion flames will yield valuable insight into cool flame chemical kinetics. The measurements proposed cannot be performed in normal gravity or in ground-based microgravity facilities. Broader Impacts: The research will be disseminated widely to the combustion research community and to industry. It should advance the state-of-the-art in cool flame kinetics mechanisms, which in turn could lead to cleaner, more efficient internal combustion engines. This project will have several educational impacts. Graduate students will conduct much of the

Rationale for Microgravity This is the ‘Justification for Testing Aboard the ISS’ section (3.1) of the experiment’s 2017 proposal in response to a solicitation from the NSF/CASIS Collaboration on Combustion and Thermal Transport Processes Research on the International Space Station to Benefit Life on Earth. The included equation is formatted differently in this copy. Previous ground-based microgravity experiments have demonstrated the scientific value of spherical, burner-supported diffusion flames. These one-dimensional flames offer a simple, fundamental configuration to improve the understanding of diffusion flame behavior and to explore such effects as transport, kinetics, soot formation, and radiation, which can be more pronounced under microgravity conditions (Atreya et al. 1992; Law et al. 2001; Lecoustre et al. 2012). Spherically-symmetric flames are not generally practical in normal gravity. This can be explained by considering the Richardson number, which is the ratio of the buoyancy force to the inertial force, Ri = g (ΔT L) / (T u2) , (1) where g is the acceleration of gravity, T is temperature, L is the characteristic length scale, and u is the characteristic velocity. Taking as representative values L = 50

the buoyancy force to the inertial force, Ri = g (ΔT L) / (T u2) , (1) where g is the acceleration of gravity, T is temperature, L is the characteristic length scale, and u is the characteristic velocity. Taking as representative values L = 50 mm, u = 5 cm/s, ΔT = 2000 K, and T = 300 K, Ri = 1300 in normal gravity. Ri can be reduced with a judicious choice of fuels and inert; Law et al. (2001) have shown that nearly spherical flames can be created in normal gravity using low pressure hydrogen inverse flames. However for typical spherical diffusion flames the only way to obtain Ri << 1 is to reduce g by four orders of magnitude. This requires a microgravity environment. Available microgravity drop tower facilities do not offer sufficient time to observe quasi-steady spherical diffusion flames, let alone their radiative extinction followed by cool diffusion flames. Experiments performed in the 5 s drop facility confirm that typical spherical diffusion flames continue growing during 5 s (see Fig. 2). Observations of cool flames in the FLEX, FLEX-2, and CFI droplet experiments involved or will involve burn times of up to 60 s. Analytical work supports these observations of slow flame development. Radial velocities in spherical diffusion flames scale with 1 / r2, where r is radius. Thus, at only a few burner diameters distance from the sphere, diffusion is the dominant transport mechanism. The characteristic diffusion time is r2/D, where D is mass diffusivity. For r = 25 mm and D = 20 mm2/s, this diffusion time is 30 s. Decreasing the

Thus, at only a few burner diameters distance from the sphere, diffusion is the dominant transport mechanism. The characteristic diffusion time is r2/D, where D is mass diffusivity. For r = 25 mm and D = 20 mm2/s, this diffusion time is 30 s. Decreasing the flame size can reduce this time, but will not permit the observation of radiative extinction followed by cool diffusion flames. Our analytical and numerical calculations indicate that approximately 30 s of jitter-free (less than 10-5 g) microgravity is needed to approach quasi-steady state for these flames. The ISS is the only microgravity platform that can provide this environment.

Science Objectives The objectives text presented here is the ‘Hypotheses and Objectives’ section (1.3) of the experiment’s 2017 proposal in response to a solicitation from the NSF/CASIS Collaboration on Combustion and Thermal Transport Processes Research on the International Space Station to Benefit Life on Earth. The hypotheses of this research are that testing aboard the ISS can demonstrate the following for the first time, contributing to an improved understanding of cool flame kinetics. 1. Steady-state cool diffusion flames on spherical porous burners. 2. Cool diffusion flames burning propane, n-butane, and n-pentane. 3. Cool diffusion flames for a wide range of Zst, Tad, and pressures. 4. Inverse cool diffusion flames. 5. Cool diffusion flames for which a decrease in fluent flow rate will cause extinction, whereas an increase will cause a transition to a hot diffusion flame, with oscillation possible between hot and cool flames. The research objectives of the proposed work are as follows. 1. Plan and support flight testing on the ISS. 2. Determine the conditions for which cool diffusion flames occur for propane, n-butane, and n-pentane; normal and inverse flames; and a broad range of Zst, Tad, and fluent flow rate. 3. Support the flight tests with advanced CFD simulations. 4. Identify or develop a chemical kinetics mechanism that yields good agreement between the CFD predictions and the ISS measurements. 5. Hardware Shortcomings CFI-G’s two primary challenges were in initiating cool flames and discerning their presence. Based on the findings of the earlier studies with droplet combustion, non-premixed cool flames can be directly ignited by limiting the ignition energy or can occur after the self-extinguishment of (normal) hot flames. Tests intended to directly ignite cool flames sometimes unintentionally resulted in hot flames. Summary of Preliminary Results Abstract for Spherical Gas-Fueled Cool Diffusion Flames: An improved understanding of cool diffusion flames could lead to improved engines. CDFs are investigated here using a spherical porous burner with gaseous fuels in the microgravity environment of the International Space Station. Normal and inverse flames burning ethane, propane, and n-butane were explored with various fuel and oxygen concentrations, pressures, and flow rates. The diagnostics included an intensified video camera, radiometers, and thermocouples. Spherical CDFs burning gases were observed for the first time. However, these CDFs were not readily produced and were only obtained for normal n-butane flames at 2 bar with an ambient oxygen mole fraction of 0.39. The hot flames that spawned the CDFs were 2.6 times as large. An analytical model is presented that combines previous models for steady droplet burning and the partial-burning regime for CDFs. The results identify the importance of burner temperature on the behavior of these CDFs. They also indicate that the observed CDFs reside in rich regions near a mixture fraction of 0.53. Abstract for Cool Diffusion Flames in a Stably Stratified Stagnation Flow: Cool diffusion flames have been a growing research topic since their discovery in 2012. Until now their study has been hindered by the high cost of the experimental systems used to observe them. A method is presented here for observing CDFs inexpensively using a pool of liquid n-heptane and parallel plates heated so as to produce a stably stratified stagnation flow. The flames were imaged with a color camera and measurements included gas phase temperatures, fuel

to observe them. A method is presented here for observing CDFs inexpensively using a pool of liquid n-heptane and parallel plates heated so as to produce a stably stratified stagnation flow. The flames were imaged with a color camera and measurements included gas phase temperatures, fuel evaporation rates, and formaldehyde emissions. These are the first observations of CDFs burning near the surface of fuel pools. The measured peak temperatures were between 705 – 760 K, which corresponds to an increase in gas temperature of 70 K. Impacts, Benefits, and Products Combustion provides 86% of the world’s energy and an even higher fraction of the energy used for transportation. The internal combustion engines used for transportation generally have thermal efficiencies of 38% or lower because of thermal losses. These efficiencies may increase to 60% if future engines can take advantage of ultra-lean combustion. However, this progress is being impeded by the limited understanding of the chemistry of cool flames. Research into cool diffusion flames (whose peak temperatures are 500 – 1000 K) has grown exponentially since they were discovered in 2012. The measurements performed for this project will help to test and advance cool flame kinetics mechanisms. This should facilitate the development of more efficient internal combustion engines. H. Introduction Tests for the Cool Flames Investigation with Gases (CFI-G) experiment are conducted in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project. As explained in the research proposal: Cool diffusion flames were discovered during droplet experiments aboard

Cool Flames Investigation with Gases (CFI-G) experiment are conducted in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project. As explained in the research proposal: Cool diffusion flames were discovered during droplet experiments aboard the International Space Station (ISS) in 2012, and this initiated a rapidly growing field of combustion research. Droplet experiments necessarily involve unsteady burning rates, so cool diffusion flames have never been observed as steady spherical flames. A natural progression toward understanding cool diffusion flames is to observe quasi-steady spherical flames on porous burners, and this is the topic of this proposal. The flames to be studied are rich in the physics and chemistry of combustion and thermal transport processes.

ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 21 November 2022 29 Most internal combustion engines are designed using computer models that neglect cool flame chemistry, but ignition and flame propagation in engines depend on cool flame chemistry. Cool flame chemistry also has a significant impact on fuel octane and cetane numbers, whose understanding has large economic consequences. The flame system to be studied will allow steady spherical cool diffusion flames to be observed for the first time. The tests, performed with gaseous fuel and a porous spherical burner, cannot be performed in normal gravity or in ground-based microgravity facilities. CFI-G had the following experimental hypotheses and experimental objective when it was proposed in 2017: Hypotheses The hypotheses of this research are that testing aboard the ISS can demonstrate the following for the first time, contributing to an improved understanding of cool flame kinetics. 1. Steady-state cool diffusion flames on spherical porous burners. 2. Cool diffusion flames burning propane, n-butane, and n-pentane. 3. Cool diffusion flames for a wide range of Zst, Tad, and pressures. 4. Inverse cool diffusion flames. 5. Cool diffusion flames for which a decrease in fluent flow rate will cause extinction, whereas an increase will cause a transition to a hot diffusion flame, with oscillation possible between hot and cool flames. Experimental Objective A. Determine the conditions for which cool diffusion flames occur for propane, n-butane, and n-pentane; normal and inverse flames; and a broad range of Zst, Tad, and fluent flow rate. where Zst and Tad are respectively the stochiometric mixture fraction and adiabatic flame temperature. However, it was later determined that the CIR facility could not support

for propane, n-butane, and n-pentane; normal and inverse flames; and a broad range of Zst, Tad, and fluent flow rate. where Zst and Tad are respectively the stochiometric mixture fraction and adiabatic flame temperature. However, it was later determined that the CIR facility could not support testing with pentane because of the fuel’s low vapor pressure so the test matrix was revised to instead include testing with ethane in addition to the propane and n-butane. The additional research objectives are as follows, where CFD stands for Computational Fluid Dynamics. B. Support the flight tests with advanced CFD simulations. C. Identify or develop a chemical kinetics mechanism that yields good agreement between the CFD predictions and the ISS measurements. D. Disseminate the results as widely as possible. The experiment is carried out using the same spherical burner configuration as ACME’s Flame Design and s-Flame (Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames) experiments. The instrumentation is the same as that used for Flame Design except that an alternate radiometer array was developed for CFI-G. Furthermore, the CFI-G tests were conducted using the

ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 21 November 2022 30 formaldehyde filter on the CFI intensified camera rather than the typically used CH* filter. In this regard, the CFI camera was developed for the Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) which preceded ACME and studied non-premixed cool flames in the combustion of liquid droplets. Microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages over normal-gravity studies. For example, the natural flicker of flames, which is a buoyancydriven (i.e., gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi-steady flames in microgravity. Characteristic length scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure. Momentum-dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion systems, can be studied at low velocities to simplify analysis. Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger sensitivity to their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics than normal-gravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment. The long residence times in microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot free. The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important. For example, chemi-ion species, electronically-excited chemiluminescent species, are at very low concentration in typical flames, making the reduced buoyancy environment valuable for evaluating the minor species chemistry. With these advantages, microgravity testing can lead to new understanding of the complex nature of combustion – regardless of the gravitational environment of the combustion application. II. testing can lead to new understanding of the complex nature of combustion – regardless of the gravitational environment of the combustion application. II. Methods/Research Operations A. Discussion of Method/Protocol The CFI-G investigation and other ACME experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew. The crew’s role is to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set of tests. The most common changes include the gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert. All testing is commanded from the ground, specifically from the Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC). The science portion of the tests were all conducted in a nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts. No CFI-G tests were conducted in a ‘manual’ mode, where changes are made to a control parameter in response to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry stream. Thus far, that has been the case for all ACME tests, with the mundane exception of ‘manually’ halting the test after the flame has extinguished or perhaps if a temperature has reached a critical value. Testing is not conducted when thrusters fire or spacecraft dock or undock from ISS to ensure an acceptable acceleration environment. Data is downlinked between each set of tests, i.e., day of testing, to allow for preliminary analysis and requisite planning for subsequent testing.

Any other difficulties in obtaining scientific data CFI-G’s two primary challenges are in initiating cool flames and discerning their presence. Based on the findings of the earlier studies with droplet combustion, nonpremixed cool flames can be directly by limiting the ignition energy or can occur after the self-extinguishment of (normal) hot flames. Tests intended to directly ignite cool flames sometimes unintentionally resulted in hot flames. A challenge for cool flame detection is concern about potential damage to the CFI intensified camera by exposing it to bright light, especially from the energized igniter, while the intensifier gain is set high. When at a small fraction (e.g., less than 10%) of the maximum flow rate, Mass Flow Controller (MFC) performance has been seen to be poor during CFI-G testing, i.e., where actual flow rate differed from that desired. Meanwhile, at high flow rates of fuel and nitrogen, the burner does not produce spherically symmetric flames. While nominally

the maximum flow rate, Mass Flow Controller (MFC) performance has been seen to be poor during CFI-G testing, i.e., where actual flow rate differed from that desired. Meanwhile, at high flow rates of fuel and nitrogen, the burner does not produce spherically symmetric flames. While nominally spherical at moderate flow rates, the flame’s center becomes increasing offset from the burner center. More specifically, the flame is shifted toward the supply tube indicating that the sintered attachment of the porous sphere to the supply tube is more ‘open’ than the pores of the spherical burner. In other words, the flow from the burner is not spherically symmetric. At sufficiently high flow rates, the flame becomes obviously non-spherical, where it can appear to be ellipsoidal or even parabolic in shape. In the latter case, the flame locally quenches near the supply tube. During Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) testing on 23 Dec. 2020, it was discovered that the lowest of the 14-micron silicon carbide fibers on the Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) fiber array had broken. Recovery plans were developed and enacted on 18 Jan. 2021 to remove the broken fragments from the harp-like array. Unfortunately, the next fiber was broken during the delicate operations where the fibers are only spaced 5 mm apart. Although ACME does have alternate arrays, it also has months of remaining testing, so the decision was made to continue testing with only 3 fibers (instead of 5) for the final BRE testing, the subsequent CLD Flame tests, and at least

In this regard, CFI-G testing is expected to continue through most of Increment 65. The cameras are sensitive to radiation where pixels gradually become ‘hot’ (i.e., dead) over time. While these bright spots are addressed in image post-processing, they are a degradation of the image quality. It is possible that the tests are subtly affected by the acceleration environment, but there is not obvious indication of this; and it has thus far not been evaluated with available measurements from the Space Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS). Recorded image data is sometimes deleted without downlinking. This is done because of operational constraints which limit the amount of data that can be managed per test day. Given the constraint, the decision is sometimes made to sacrifice some image data to allow additional tests to be conducted. This is intentionally done in order to maximize the scientific return of each day of testing within the project constraints. D. the U. of Maryland investigator team and lightly edited by Stocker] Data sets of spherical diffusion flames as a function of the fuel mass flow rate, atmospheric O2 concentration, fuel dilution, and pressure were obtained. The raw test measurements made from devices - such as thermocouples, photomultiplier tubes (PMTs), gas flow meters, and radiometers - were saved in a csv file format per each test. The data rate of the non-imaging measurements was 125 per sec. The raw data was processed to transform it into scientific measurements. In addition, test images recorded in tiff and hobj formats respectively for the CFI intensified camera and ACME DataCam have been analyzed to find flame diameters. Of these the intensified camera is of most value and all of its images to date have been converted to video files and reviewed. Maryland investigator team] The first three days of testing have yielded dozens of flames, some lasting several minutes. Based on the output from the photomultipliers, radiometers, and intensified camera images we do not believe any self-sustained cool flames were created. While it is possible that momentary cool flames were created, these are difficult to detect without increasing the gain on the intensified camera before the hot flames extinguish, which is planned. The video record will furnish excellent measurements of flame diameter versus time for a broad range of fuels and conditions. These will be compared with a simple analytical model and detailed CFD simulations using Sphdif. Thin-filament pyrometry has been performed and the results will soon be analyzed. F. Introduction Tests for the Cool Flames Investigation with Gases (CFI-G) experiment are conducted in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project. As explained in the research proposal: Cool diffusion flames were discovered during droplet experiments aboard the International Space Station (ISS) in 2012, and this initiated a rapidly growing field of combustion research. Droplet experiments necessarily involve unsteady burning rates, so cool diffusion flames have never been observed as steady spherical flames. A natural progression toward understanding cool diffusion flames is to observe quasi-steady spherical flames on porous burners, and this is the topic of this proposal. The flames to be studied are rich in the physics and chemistry of combustion and thermal transport processes.

ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 21 November 2022 36 Most internal combustion engines are designed using computer models that neglect cool flame chemistry, but ignition and flame propagation in engines depend on cool flame chemistry. Cool flame chemistry also has a significant impact on fuel octane and cetane numbers, whose understanding has large economic consequences. The flame system to be studied will allow steady spherical cool diffusion flames to be observed for the first time. The tests, performed with gaseous fuel and a porous spherical burner, cannot be performed in normal gravity or in ground-based microgravity facilities. CFI-G had the following experimental hypotheses and experimental objective when it was proposed in 2017: Hypotheses The hypotheses of this research are that testing aboard the ISS can demonstrate the following for the first time, contributing to an improved understanding of cool flame kinetics. 1. Steady-state cool diffusion flames on spherical porous burners. 2. Cool diffusion flames burning propane, n-butane, and n-pentane. 3. Cool diffusion flames for a wide range of Zst, Tad, and pressures. 4. Inverse cool diffusion flames. 5. Cool diffusion flames for which a decrease in fluent flow rate will cause extinction, whereas an increase will cause a transition to a hot diffusion flame, with oscillation possible between hot and cool flames. Experimental Objective A. Determine the conditions for which cool diffusion flames occur for propane, n-butane, and n-pentane; normal and inverse flames; and a broad range of Zst, Tad, and fluent flow rate. where Zst and Tad are respectively the stochiometric mixture fraction and adiabatic flame temperature. However, it was later determined that the CIR facility could not support

However, it was later determined that the CIR facility could not support testing with pentane because of the fuel’s low vapor pressure so the test matrix was revised to instead include testing with ethane in addition to the propane and n-butane. The additional research objectives are as follows, where CFD stands for Computational Fluid Dynamics. B. Support the flight tests with advanced CFD simulations. C. The experiment is carried out using the same spherical burner configuration as ACME’s Flame Design and s-Flame (Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames) experiments. The instrumentation is the same as that used for Flame Design except that an alternate radiometer array was developed for CFI-G. Furthermore, the CFI-G tests were conducted using the

ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 21 November 2022 37 formaldehyde filter on the CFI intensified camera rather than the typically used CH* filter. In this regard, the CFI camera was developed for the Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) which preceded ACME and studied non-premixed cool flames in the combustion of liquid droplets. Microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages over normal-gravity studies. For example, the natural flicker of flames, which is a buoyancydriven (i.e., gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi-steady flames in microgravity. Characteristic length scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure. Momentum-dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion systems, can be studied at low velocities to simplify analysis. Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger sensitivity to their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics than normal-gravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment. The long residence times in microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot free. The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important. For example, chemi-ion species, electronically-excited chemiluminescent species, are at very low concentration in typical flames, making the reduced buoyancy environment valuable for evaluating the minor species chemistry. With these advantages, microgravity testing can lead to new understanding of the complex nature of combustion – regardless of the gravitational environment of the combustion application. VI. Discussion of Method/Protocol The CFI-G investigation and other ACME experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew. The crew’s role is to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set of tests. The most common changes include the gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert. All testing is commanded from the ground, specifically from the Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC). The science portion of the tests were all conducted in a nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts. No CFI-G tests were conducted in a ‘manual’ mode, where changes are made to a control parameter in response to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry stream. Thus far, that has been the case for all ACME tests, with the mundane exception of ‘manually’ halting the test after the flame has extinguished or perhaps if a temperature has reached a critical value. Testing is not conducted when thrusters fire or spacecraft dock or undock from ISS to ensure an acceptable acceleration environment. Data is downlinked between each set of tests, i.e., day of testing, to allow for preliminary analysis and requisite planning for subsequent testing.

These are simple hydrocarbon gases for which the hot flame chemistry is reasonably well understood, but where there is much remaining to be learned about the cool flame chemistry. Mission anomalies On Aug. 30 (GMT 242), the primary Image Processing and Storage Unit, used to record the imaging from both the ACME DataCam and CFI intensified camera (IPSU-G, also known as IPSU5), caused issues and eventually stopped working. Only the first two tests on that day were successful, where two tests aborted due to an IPSU error, and three tests failed to ignite. In closing checkout, it was determined that the hot-wire igniter tip had also failed. With the IPSU-G failure, the test day was nearly a total loss. Except for a small number of sample images downloaded during the midst of testing, the primary image data from even the successful tests was lost. Furthermore, there was no more propane available for use in inverse-flame testing, so the test day could not be repeated. However, astronaut Mark Vande Hei replaced the failed igniter tip on Sept. 8 and the failed hard drive in the IPSU-G on Sept. 10, and CFI-G testing successfully resumed on Sept. 13, just 2 weeks after the double failure. It is likely that the closest thermocouple, approximately 1 cm from the burner surface, was a factor in the reignition. Example CFI-G Inverse Butane Flame This example image can be readily identified as an inverse flame because the soot is outside, rather than inside, of the flame. The soot is formed when the fuel combines with itself at high temperatures in the absence of oxygen. In this regard, the inverse flame is like a bubble separating the outer fuel from the inner oxygen, where the two reactants are consumed producing light, heat, and chemical products (e.g., carbon dioxide and water vapor). Flames of hydrocarbon fuels are naturally blue, while the hightemperature soot glows red, orange, yellow, or even white depending on its temperature. At ignition, this flame was all bright and sooty, but the system is not fully symmetric. There is some asymmetry to the burner flow, and there is heat loss to the tube supplying the gas to the porous spherical burner. As a result, the soot faded from the lower hemisphere, which in this image appears to be soot free. Meanwhile, the upper hemisphere remained enveloped in a layer of glowing soot. Tests like this have yielded valuable data for improving our understanding of how to control soot generation. The purpose of this extra day was to recreate the test conditions in which we achieved cool flames in earlier testing, and we successfully achieved cool flames! In two tests, the butane hot flames extinguished due to radiative heat loss, but then seconds later they reignited. This extinction and reignition occurred several times during each of these tests. The butane reignited because a cool flame occurred between the hot flames. Cool flame chemistry is important for ignition in internal combustion engines and an improved understanding would aid the development of vehicles that experience less wear on engine parts, get better gas mileage, and create less pollution. Summary of the ISS data collection The CFI-G data is all digital and includes both image and non-image data, where this is true for the other ACME experiments. To be clear, there was no collection of soot or other physical samples that were subsequently transported to the ground. The CFI-G image data includes images from the following cameras: 1. ACME DataCam, used with a clear fused-silica ‘filter’ and various zoom and focus settings (but those settings were consistent within each individual test) 2. CFI intensified camera, used always (or at least nearly so) with a formaldehyde filter for CFI-G 3. High-Bitdepth Multispectral (HiBMs) camera, equipped with a red filter corresponding to the opposing CIR illumination package, which was sometimes left off The raw DataCam images are in a Halcon Iconic Object (hobj) format, while the images from the CFI, and HiBMs cameras are provided in a Tagged Image File (tif) format. In contrast, the analog video was recorded on the ground in a Transport Stream (ts) format. The key non-imaging data from a test is a comma-delimited file that is described in detail in the Software Interface Design Description (ACME-DOC-010 Rev. D). The raw data is currently archived at NASA and work is underway to make it available publicly through NASA’s Physical Science Informatics System (PSI).

20 August 2018 Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) PURPOSE: ACME is focused on advanced combustion technology via fundamental microgravity research. The primary goal is to improve efficiency and reduce pollutant emission in practical terrestrial combustion. A secondary objective is fire prevention, especially for spacecraft. RESEARCH: ACME includes six independent experiments investigating laminar, non-premixed flames of gaseous fuels. The experiments are being conducted with a single set of modular hardware in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station (ISS). While the ISS astronauts set up the experimental hardware, the ACME tests are remotely commanded from NASA’s Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center. STATUS: ACME setup and checkout were carried out by the ISS crew in Sept.-Oct. 2017. Thus far, a dozen astronauts from Germany, Italy, Japan, Russia and the United States have supported the ACME research. Since November 2017, over 300 flames have been ignited for the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) and Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) experiments led respectively by Profs. Marshall B. Long (Yale University) and Derek Dunn-Rankin (University of California, Irvine). A second round of CLD Flame tests is currently underway and should end in September when the testing will transition back to the E-FIELD Flames experiment. In late 2018, the hardware will be reconfigured for the Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) experiment led by Prof. Jim Quintiere (University of Maryland). While the first two ACME experiments are focused on improving practical combustion on Earth, BRE is aimed at improving spacecraft fire safety. CH* is an excited species and emits blue light as it drops to a lower energy level in a process known as chemiluminescence. It is the primary source of the blue that is the natural color of hydrocarbon flames (neglecting the broadband thermal radiation from the soot). Diffusion flames with a weak air coflow as a function of the electric field strength, where an open copper mesh above the flame is negatively and positively charged in the top and bottom rows, respectively. Flames naturally include ions which can be affected by a powerful electric or magnetic field. In ACME’s E-FIELD Flames experiment, the copper mesh is energized up to 10,000 volts. This technology could be used to stabilize fuel-lean flames under conditions which are less polluting.

This Researcher’s Guide is intended to help potential ISS combustion science researchers plan experiments utilizing the microgravity environment in order to understand how heat and mass transport phenomena coupled with chemistry affect combustion behavior and fire safety. 5 1. Microgravity, or weightlessness, alters many observable phenomena within the physical and life sciences. Systems and processes affected by microgravity include surface wetting and interfacial tension, multiphase flow and heat transfer, multiphase system dynamics, solidification, and fire phenomena and combustion. Microgravity induces a vast array of changes in organisms ranging from bacteria to humans, including global alterations in gene expression and 3-D aggregation of cells into tissue-like architecture. 2. Extreme conditions in the ISS environment include exposure to extreme heat and cold cycling, ultra-vacuum, atomic oxygen, and high-energy radiation. Testing and qualification of materials exposed to these extreme conditions have provided data to enable the manufacturing of longlife, reliable components used on Earth as well as in the world’s most sophisticated satellite and spacecraft components. 3. Low-Earth orbit at 51 degrees inclination and at a 90-minute orbit affords ISS a unique vantage point with an altitude of approximately 240 miles (400 kilometers) and an orbital path over 90 percent of the Earth’s population. This can provide improved spatial resolution and variable lighting conditions compared to the sun-synchronous orbits of typical Earth remote-sensing satellites. 8 Combustion occurs when fuel and oxygen react to produce carbon dioxide, water and heat. For the foreseeable future, the overwhelming majority of delivered energy in terrestrial applications will be from combustion or other chemically reacting systems. These energy uses cover the range from electric power and transportation to processes directly tied to the delivered material (e.g., glass and steel manufacture). These processes produce some of the most important environmental hazards currently facing humanity (global climate change, acid gas pollution, mercury contamination from coal, and wild-land fires). Despite being the subject of active research for over 80 years, combustion processes remain one of the most poorly controlled phenomena that have a significant impact on human health, comfort and safety. This is because the simplest combustor (e.g., kitchen stove) remains beyond our detailed numerical modeling capabilities. Typically, the combustion process involves a large number of chemical species (hundreds) and reactions (even thousands). It is these species and reactions that determine flammability limits (combustor operating ranges) and pollutant emissions. Much of combustion research involves developing a comprehensive and predictive quantitative understanding of this complex process. This understanding usually occurs in smaller, bench-scale experiments that are amenable to detailed study and modeling. In these bench-scale experiments, however, buoyant forces, created by gravity and the large temperature differential between the flame and the ambient gas, dominate and frequently obscure the physical and chemical phenomena of interest, and hence, complicate analyses. In the absence of gravity, buoyancy can be suppressed, and the analyses can be reduced to much simpler onedimensional systems. To understand the strong influence of gravity on flames, one can consider the

frequently obscure the physical and chemical phenomena of interest, and hence, complicate analyses. In the absence of gravity, buoyancy can be suppressed, and the analyses can be reduced to much simpler onedimensional systems. To understand the strong influence of gravity on flames, one can consider the density gradients in flames. Typical flame temperatures are on the order of 2,300 degrees Kelvin, whereas ambient temperatures are approximately 300 degrees Kelvin. This produces an eight-fold density change over the scale of a centimeter. The resultant density gradient induces a strong velocity field that dominates all but the highest flow fields. This flow field causes the flame to lift and point upward. The resultant flow instabilities cause the flicker typical of flames on Earth. Figure 1 contains a gallery of 1-g to 0-g comparison flames. By varying or eliminating the effects of gravity, we can extract fundamental data that are important for understanding combustion systems. This approach has been implemented to some extent in existing terrestrial reduced-gravity platforms, but the experimental time scales and sizes have been limited. Long-duration Why Conduct Combustion Research in Microgravity?

9 experiments using realistic sizes are essential for a comprehensive understanding of the combustion phenomena and are possible only in the microgravity environments offered by space facilities. Besides terrestrial applications of combustion, gravity-related combustion research issues are also of crucial importance to NASA’s manned and unmanned missions. Fire safety is an important operational element of human space exploration missions to minimize the likelihood and impact of accidental fires in spacecraft and human habitats. The effects of these environmental changes on combustion in reduced gravity are unclear and need to be better understood for all missionrelevant scenarios. Every aspect of fire prevention, detection and suppression is Figure 1. 1-g and 0-g comparison flames. Left to right, top to bottom: ethane jet flames, ethylene jet flames, candle flames, burning heptane droplets and flame spread over a butanol pool. (Image credit: NASA)

10 fundamentally different in space than on Earth. Thus, an improved knowledge of combustion in reduced gravity is essential to adapt fire safety concepts and systems to the more stringent conditions of the space environment. Benefits of conducting combustion research in microgravity can thus be summarized as: • Removal of the complex interaction between the buoyant flow and the energy feedback to the flame. • Realistic simulation of the fire risk seen in manned spacecraft. • Practical simulation of the gravitational environment seen for reacting systems in future spacecraft.

11 Over the past two decades, microgravity combustion research has focused primarily on increasing our understanding of fundamental combustion processes (e.g., droplet combustion, soot production, flame spread, smoldering and gas jet flames). This research program has been highly successful and was aided by synergistic programs in Europe and in Japan. Overall improvements were made in the ability to model droplet combustion in spray combustors (e.g., jet engines), predict flame spread, predict soot production, and detection and prevention of spacecraft fires. Some of the findings from past microgravity combustion research are presented below. Current ongoing flight projects on the International Space Station (ISS) are given in each area. Droplet Combustion The availability of a long-duration, high-quality microgravity environment allows researchers to study the textbook problem of a spherical droplet surrounded by a spherical flame in an infinite, quiescent, ambient atmosphere. A cadre of researchers from academia, industry and federal laboratories has successfully established this simple geometry as an excellent test bed to study fundamental combustion science problems and other topics of applied combustion research. Through a robust program, researchers gained insight into wide-ranging problems of interest in combustion science. These programs included ground-based experimental work in drop towers and aircraft flying parabolic trajectories (and normal gravity; i.e., 1-g, test laboratories), numerical and theoretical modeling, and ultimately experiments in space-based facilities. The programs provided the opportunity to investigate phenomena such as: • Departures from quasi-steady combustion. • Transition from diffusive to radiative extinction. • Liquid-phase transport. • The influence of convection on flame dynamics (refer to Figure 2). • The dynamics of soot formation and destruction (refer to Figure 3). •
